chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: Adding taps to Eleanor Powell's ballet turns
summary: He shows her how to put taps in the snatch and pivot, and says he still uses a step he taught her in his Caravan dance.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: So she showed me some of the steps. She said she had never used taps on her shoes before, and for me to watch and see what I thought of it and could I finish up some of the routine. And she explained that she had to be in Hollywood
in two weeks, you see. So --
This is before Eleanor Powell had learned any tap dancing? This was her first introduction to tap dancing?
Yes, that was it. See, she was taking from Mr. Buddy Bradley.
So you initially went to New York and were hanging around the Buddy Bradley-Billy Pierce Studio?
Yeah, Billy Pierce Studio, you see.
How long were you hanging around there before Eleanor Powell came in?
Oh, about two -- two days. She came in about the third day we were there, you know.

Well, maybe -- well, tell me the story about Eleanor Powell, but I'm interested in what was -- what was the Buddy Bradley-Billy Pierce Studio like? First tell me the Eleanor Powell story. What happened with that and what you taught her?

Well, I taught her -- I taught her about a chorus and a half of how she could tap -- she could do like the same ballet and put the taps to the ballet, you see. See, because she was a champion ballet -- tap -- ballet dancer. She was really was a champion. You could understand everything she did, even if you never did any ballet yourself or anything, you know.

Well, my mother's dance teacher was also a ballet dancer, you know, and she was some kind of an authority of that dance. And so I understood it. But I explained to Eleanor Powell how she could get rhythm with the ballet, and she wouldn't have to, you know, not do ballet dancing, see, because, I mean, these spins and pivots and pirouettes and things, you know, and leaps, anything, see, told her how she could get the taps in there. So that's what I was teaching her, you know.
Which you will notice, when she dances, she does lots of turns with taps on, tap turns, which -- a girl, you know, (inaudible) would have to have ballet to be able to do pirouettes.
Was this something that you choreographed yourself in terms of the amount of taps?
Yeah. Yeah.
Can you demonstrate to show me what those taps were like? In a turn? Or what exactly -- what rhythms did you show her?

Yeah, well, I showed her how to do snatches, you see. See, in ballet there's a snatch, what they got -- I call it a snatch because it is --it really is a preparation for a pivot, you see. Now, one foot goes out. The left foot goes out, and it comes back to the right foot, and then a spin occurs. A pivot occurs.
Well, that's what I showed her, how to do, add sound to this. As the foot go out, you know, she can make a sound, you know, like --
(Tap interlude)

-- like that, you see. And then cross over with the right foot and then convey the pivot, see, because she could actually, when she spinned, she could spin like -- she'd go around six times. By the time an ordinary person would turn once, she could spin about six times with the head, you know, one, two, three, four, five six, like that, and I heard the beat. I could see the beat actually, you know. And I knew it was a sound. So that's what I was teaching her, you know.

And I still do one of the steps I taught her. I even do it now, I mean, and I do a dance to the melody of 'Caravan,' you see, that's a Duke Ellington melody, and I do some of the Eleanor Powell tap in that, see, that I taught her for Mr. Buddy Bradley, because he wasn't there.
